title: EXOhSPEC: compact active control, fibre tests, and an unresolved deployment status
reading_boundary: Seven selected design, laboratory, calibration and official-status sources. No completed on-sky stellar-RV performance paper for the Thai National Telescope instrument was identified in this reading set.
current_status: Current NARIT pages conflict: the technology page says installed and tested with the 2.4 m telescope, while the Thai National Observatory roster labels EXOhSPEC under development. The earlier ING deployment was decommissioned in May 2024.
short_summary: EXOhSPEC's published path demonstrates a compact high-resolution prototype, laboratory active control, fibre modal-noise tests and a thermally controlled metalon experiment. These results belong to specific laboratory or prototype configurations and do not yet establish long-term stellar precision for the Thai instrument.
latest_problem: The 2025 metalon experiment measured 8 m/s temporal drift over 470 to 780 nm, or 5 m/s after polynomial flattening, while the spectrograph's active stabilization was not engaged. Current NARIT pages also disagree on whether the telescope instrument is installed and tested or still under development.
lessons: Design requirements, laboratory image-motion tests and stellar time-series precision are different evidence classes.
The approximately 4 m/s result describes a compact laboratory prototype, not a completed on-sky performance programme.
Modal-noise mitigation carries a measured throughput trade-off and remains dependent on fibre and illumination configuration.
Thermal stability of a calibrator enclosure does not by itself establish the drift of the complete spectrograph path.
A physical deployment and its current operating state must be checked against dated facility evidence rather than inferred from an instrument paper.

title: EXPRES: design, measured performance, and the long-baseline stability problem
reading_boundary: A selected reading path through 13 primary papers. It is not a complete bibliography of every science paper that used EXPRES.
current_status: Lowell's 2026A observer material lists EXPRES as available, including remote observing, after prior commissioning and general-use phases.
short_summary: EXPRES demonstrates that excellent short-term calibration and sub-m/s stellar residuals do not guarantee multi-year stability. Later work increasingly treats wavelength calibration, stellar line-shape change and instrument state as linked time-series problems.
latest_problem: The 2026 seven-year study found a coherent 2.8 m/s trough-to-peak drift around the 2022 temperature excursion. A regression using echellogram geometry, comb-line shapes and telemetry reduced the solar trend RMS from 1.32 to 0.43 m/s, but a deployable correction still needs era-aware validation and planet-signal preservation tests.
lessons: A calibration residual, a formal photon error and stellar time-series RMS answer different questions.
Dense laser-frequency-comb information can improve wavelength models, but the resulting change in stellar RMS can be much smaller than the calibration improvement.
Activity-correction methods can lower scatter while disagreeing on the corrected velocities; injected-signal recovery and interpretable diagnostics are therefore essential.
Simultaneous solar observations across instruments provide a practical way to distinguish astrophysical variability from instrument-specific behaviour.
Long-baseline maintenance, temperature and detector-state changes must be modelled as data eras rather than assumed stationary.

future_analysis.title: Era-aware EXPRES correction audit with planet-preservation tests
future_analysis.status: future analysis question, not completed research, a publication claim, or an endorsed instrument programme
future_analysis.question: Can a correction learned from instrument-state diagnostics remain valid across maintenance and temperature regimes while preserving low-amplitude Keplerian signals?
future_analysis.basis: This extends the validation questions raised by the 2022 method comparison and the diagnostics demonstrated in the 2026 long-baseline study.
steps: Align science and solar RVs with laser-comb image shifts, scale and rotation, comb-line bisectors, environmental telemetry and maintenance dates.

Fit a small interpretable baseline first, then compare it with nonlinear models using the same blocked folds.
Inject Keplerian signals before correction across period, phase and semi-amplitude; report recovery bias, completeness and false positives.
Emit per-exposure state flags, correction uncertainty and an out-of-distribution warning instead of silently correcting unfamiliar states.
Reproduce the published solar and quiet-star checks before proposing any scientific use.
success_tests: Lower held-out solar and quiet-star scatter without absorbing injected Keplerian amplitude.
Stable coefficients or documented model changes across instrument eras.
No improvement claim based only on training-set RMS.
Reproducible figures and machine-readable fold assignments.

title: HARPS: calibration structure, instrument eras, and the 2026 hardware change
reading_boundary: Six selected technical and methods sources, not a complete bibliography of the HARPS planet surveys or all papers using archival spectra.
current_status: ESO records that HARPS returned to normal operations on 20 June 2026 after a detector, electronics, cooling and fibre upgrade; its atmospheric-dispersion corrector was then listed out of operation on 3 July.
short_summary: HARPS established the stable, fibre-fed architecture used by later precision-RV instruments. Its literature also gives a clear warning against treating a long archive as one homogeneous time series: calibration changes, the 2015 fibre exchange and the 2026 detector-era change create measurable boundaries.
latest_problem: The 2026 upgrade replaced several coupled subsystems at once. ESO has posted operational notices and a work-in-progress performance file, but the checked page says a final report will follow. Any cross-era correction should therefore be measured from standards and overlapping diagnostics rather than assumed from the earlier instrument.
lessons: Resolving power and spectrograph stability enable precise RV extraction but do not themselves define long-term accuracy.
Laser-comb tests exposed local wavelength-solution structure that a single global residual could hide.
The 2015 octagonal fibres improved illumination scrambling and throughput while introducing a star-dependent velocity offset.
Calibration solutions must be versioned on both sides of hardware changes; one offset is not automatically valid for every spectrum.
The 2026 detector, electronics, cooling and fibre work begins another measurement era whose transfer function still needs a final public characterization.

future_analysis.title: HARPS 2015-to-2026 era transfer notebook

future_analysis.basis: The 2015 fibre report measured spectral-type-dependent offsets, while the 2019 calibration paper treats the pre/post-2015 solutions separately and ESO now documents a new 2026 era.

Recovered injected amplitudes remain unbiased within their stated uncertainty.
Results change transparently when masks or spectral-type groupings change.
No post-2026 performance claim precedes the final instrument characterization.

title: ESPRESSO: on-sky precision, wavelength accuracy, and light-path validation
reading_boundary: Seven selected instrument, calibration, science and status sources. This is not a complete bibliography of ESPRESSO science programmes.
current_status: ESO lists ESPRESSO as offered, and its instrument news states that the laser frequency comb returned to full operations in November 2025 with updated performance guidance in 2026.
short_summary: ESPRESSO demonstrates sub-m/s on-sky measurements in several contexts, while its calibration literature exposes a second problem: internal sources can be precise without independently validating the entire path followed by stellar light. The temporary iodine-cell experiment turns that distinction into a practical end-to-end test.
latest_problem: The 2025 iodine-cell study reported sub-0.20 m/s end-to-end stability in its experiment but only few-m/s absolute wavelength accuracy, and found sensitivity to fibre-injection geometry. ESO separately records that laser-comb background variability affected line shapes before the comb returned to full operation. These results motivate a monitoring tool that reports precision, accuracy and illumination sensitivity separately.
lessons: The 0.10 m/s instrumental scale inferred at commissioning is not the same as every stellar time-series RMS.
Photon uncertainty, filtered short-cadence RMS and planet-model residuals answer different questions.
A dense internal calibrator can reveal structure but does not automatically validate the telescope-to-product science path.
Absolute wavelength accuracy for fundamental-constant work and differential repeatability for exoplanet RV work require different tests.
Calibration-source state and fibre-injection geometry should be explicit metadata rather than hidden pipeline assumptions.

future_analysis.title: ESPRESSO calibration-consistency monitor
future_analysis.status: future analysis question, not completed research and dependent on access to suitable calibration and engineering products
future_analysis.question: Can an open diagnostic compare ThAr, Fabry-Perot, laser-comb and occasional end-to-end reference measurements without confusing precision with absolute accuracy?
future_analysis.basis: The 2021 calibration comparison maps structured solution differences, the 2025 iodine experiment tests the science path, and ESO's dated notices show that calibrator state changes with time.
steps: Version every exposure by DRS, observing mode, calibrator state and fibre-injection configuration.
Compute order- and detector-position residual maps between available calibration families.
Track line-shape, background and wavelength residual summaries through time with maintenance boundaries.
Evaluate differential repeatability and absolute accuracy as separate outputs.
Hold out complete nights and hardware states; flag unfamiliar configurations rather than extrapolating silently.
Test whether any proposed correction preserves injected Doppler shifts before applying it to science targets.
success_tests: Reproduce published calibration comparisons on the same data definition.
Detect known state changes without using science outcomes as labels.
Preserve injected shifts across wavelength and illumination conditions.
Publish uncertainties and missing-metadata flags with every diagnostic.

title: HARPS-N: wavelength solutions, solar curation, and decade-scale interpretation
reading_boundary: Six selected instrument, calibration, solar and current-status sources. It is not a complete bibliography of HARPS-N planet and atmosphere studies.
current_status: TNG's AOT54 material lists HARPS-N for normal service or visitor operation and GIARPS without restrictions.
short_summary: HARPS-N's solar programme shows why a stable spectrograph still needs evolving reduction and explicit data curation. Revised wavelength solutions improved three-year daily scatter, while the decade release identifies hardware and observing-quality boundaries and separates daily granulation from the solar magnetic cycle.
latest_problem: The decade release retains 109466 spectra after rejecting 30 percent affected by weather or understood systematics. It reports 0.49 m/s median daily RMS, 2.95 m/s raw decade RMS, and 0.41 m/s after modelling the magnetic-cycle contribution. Those values describe different selections and corrections; a reusable pipeline needs machine-readable rejection reasons and leakage tests.
lessons: A wavelength solution can change by tens of m/s locally while the combined stellar RV changes much less.
Using calibrations closer in time and selecting stable ThAr lines reduced a measurable pipeline contribution.
Rejecting weather and hardware intervals is part of the measurement definition, not clerical cleaning.
Daily solar granulation and a decade magnetic cycle occupy different timescales and require different validation.
Contemporaneous instruments provide a stronger systematics test than one instrument fitted in isolation.

future_analysis.title: HARPS-N solar quality-mask and signal-preservation audit
future_analysis.status: future analysis question, not completed research and dependent on released spectra plus sufficient event metadata
future_analysis.question: Can every rejected or corrected solar interval be represented by an auditable quality flag while preserving injected rotation and planet-like signals?
future_analysis.basis: The three-year paper links improvement to wavelength recipes and calibration timing; the decade release adds explicit weather, drift, blaze and hardware curation across a much longer baseline.

Reproduce the published sample counts and daily statistics from the released products.
Train no correction on the held-out year used for evaluation.
Inject sinusoids before curation across rotation and habitable-zone periods and measure attenuation.
Compare HARPS-N residuals with overlapping NEID days to separate shared solar structure from local effects.
Publish a sensitivity table showing how each flag changes cadence, RMS and recovered amplitude.
success_tests: Published counts and summary statistics reproduce within documented rounding.
Every excluded observation has a human-readable reason and source field.
Held-out signal recovery is reported alongside any RMS improvement.
Results remain traceable to raw product IDs and pipeline versions.

title: NEID: environmental stability, illumination, solar baselines, and RV eras
reading_boundary: Seven selected subsystem, operations, solar and pipeline sources. It is not a complete bibliography of NEID exoplanet results.
current_status: WIYN describes NEID as commissioned and in full science operation; current proposal information documents the shared queue and long-term programmes.
short_summary: NEID couples sub-mK environmental control with a fibre system designed to suppress illumination errors that a wavelength reference cannot necessarily calibrate. Its public solar archive and versioned DRP records make it suitable for testing how weather, hardware events, master files and barycentric or extinction treatment propagate into RV products.
latest_problem: Current DRP documentation says the ThAr master wavelength solution has known systematics near order edges and versions etalon line lists around 2024 and 2025 changes. The 3.5-year solar release identifies 117060 usable observations, but curation alone does not show whether a correction preserves weak Doppler signals.
lessons: A 0.4 mK laboratory thermal result is not a stellar RV measurement.
Illumination changes can create errors that do not share the calibrator's optical path.
The 0.27 m/s value is a single-visit instrument requirement, not a universal achieved RMS.
Solar RMS depends visibly on sky-quality selection and time baseline.
Hardware events and master calibration files define RV eras that must accompany reduced data.

future_analysis.title: NEID RV-era and calibration-master validation notebook
future_analysis.status: future analysis question, not completed research and dependent on archive products and confirmed event metadata
future_analysis.question: Can a version-aware validation notebook detect order-edge and era-dependent shifts while separating weather and solar variability from instrument changes?
future_analysis.basis: The fibre paper identifies uncalibratable illumination paths, the cross-instrument study exposes a late-day trend, and DRP 1.5.2 publishes explicit wavelength-master limitations and RV eras.
steps: Join every solar and standard-star product to DRP version, RV era, wavelength master, etalon list and observing conditions.
Measure residuals by order position and barycentric velocity before pooling a scalar RV.
Test late-day or high-airmass trends against overlapping EXPRES and HARPS-N solar observations.
Hold out complete hardware eras and nights when comparing correction models.
Inject wavelength-dependent Doppler shifts and verify recovery after masking or correction.
Emit an era card and out-of-scope warning with every result.
success_tests: Known era boundaries are recovered without using planet-fit residuals as labels.
Order-edge diagnostics improve on a held-out era rather than only the training period.
Injected amplitudes remain unbiased within stated uncertainty.
Every output records data IDs, DRP and master-file versions.

title: KPF: solar diagnostics, reduction eras, and the 2026 vacuum-system outage
reading_boundary: Five selected design, instrument, solar, pipeline and current-status sources. It is not a complete KPF science bibliography.
current_status: Keck's current status page says KPF is offline until further notice after an April 2026 turbo-pump failure.
short_summary: KPF combines a broad optical science channel, solar feed and dense calibration with a pipeline that explicitly tracks service missions and instrument eras. Early solar comparisons measured several-hour agreement with NEID, while later hardware and reduction changes prevent a single stationary interpretation.
latest_problem: The instrument is currently unavailable after a vacuum-pump failure. Pipeline releases also document evolving era definitions, master calibrations and order-trace fixes, so post-repair products will require an explicit new validation boundary.
lessons: A 0.50 m/s requirement and 0.30 m/s goal are engineering targets, not achieved stellar RMS.
Several-hour solar agreement with NEID is valuable but cannot establish multi-year accuracy.
Solar data exposed early detector and wavelength-calibration problems that a headline precision would hide.
Pipeline era and service-mission identifiers are part of the scientific measurement definition.
A return from a vacuum intervention should begin a new validation era rather than inherit pre-failure performance.

future_analysis.status: future analysis question, not completed research and blocked on post-repair data
future_analysis.question: Can public solar products and pipeline metadata reproduce known early issues and quantify changes across service missions without absorbing solar signals?
future_analysis.basis: SoCal provides dense public observations while the pipeline and status pages expose dated changes that can define held-out eras.
steps: Join each solar product to pipeline version, KPF era, service mission, calibration master and quality flags.
Reproduce the several-hour KPF–NEID comparison before extending the baseline.
Hold out complete service-mission eras and inject wavelength-dependent shifts before correction.
Start a separate post-repair validation only after new data and a dated return notice exist.

Injected amplitudes remain unbiased in held-out periods.

Every output records pipeline and instrument-era identifiers.

title: MAROON-X: short-term precision, run offsets, and interrupted instrument baselines
reading_boundary: Six selected design, commissioning, operations, incident and long-baseline sources. Science applications are not exhaustively catalogued.
current_status: Gemini's 2026B material schedules MAROON-X in fixed visiting-instrument blocks; the 2024 incident notice warns that existing 2024A reductions were uncertain at about 20 m/s.
short_summary: MAROON-X moved from a sub-m/s design to regular short-term 0.30 m/s instrumental performance. Its later literature shows the harder problem: etalon drift, run offsets, earthquakes, power loss and reduction changes interrupt the long baseline.
latest_problem: The 2025 ensemble study inferred run offsets to about 0.5 m/s and obtained below 0.70 m/s residual RMS for HD 3651 over 29 months. Gemini separately reports two 2024A image shifts that left existing reductions uncertain near 20 m/s.
lessons: Short-term instrumental precision does not control offsets between observing runs.
A slowly drifting etalon can be precise within a night while moving the long-term reference.
Reference-star ensembles add information but also inherit assumptions about stellar variability.
Earthquakes and power events create physical and reduction-era boundaries.
Injection recovery is necessary when corrections are learned from the same time series.

future_analysis.title: MAROON-X run-offset and incident-era audit
future_analysis.status: future analysis question, not completed research and dependent on released era metadata
future_analysis.question: How stable is the published ensemble-offset method when entire stars, runs and the 2024 incident era are held out?
future_analysis.basis: The 2025 study supplies a tested ensemble framework, while Gemini identifies two external events requiring a distinct validation era.
steps: Encode run, detector, etalon and incident boundaries before fitting offsets.
Repeat leave-one-star-out and leave-one-run-out tests with published injection settings.
Compare corrected red and blue channel residuals without pooling them prematurely.
Treat 2024A as a separate recovery test and publish blocked states where reprocessed products are absent.
success_tests: Held-out run offsets remain within stated uncertainty.
Injected long-period amplitudes survive the correction.
The 2024A result is never mixed with unaffected 2024B data.
Reference-star assumptions are explicit and sensitivity-tested.

title: CARMENES: two-channel information, nightly zero points, and chromatic activity
reading_boundary: Seven selected instrument, pipeline, survey, activity, precision and availability sources. It is not a complete planet or atmosphere bibliography.
current_status: Calar Alto's current 2026 call offers the 3.5 m telescope, and the CARMENES instrument page provides open-time observing instructions.
short_summary: CARMENES joins visible and near-infrared velocities, but their information content and systematic limits are not identical. Public DR1 products expose nightly zero-point corrections, and chromatic indicators help test whether signals arise from stellar line changes.
latest_problem: DR1 uses nightly zero points derived from quiet stars, substituting adjacent-night averages when a direct value is unavailable. Later work still describes unexplained night-to-night jumps of a few m/s, so the correction and its uncertainty remain part of any planet search.
lessons: The VIS and NIR channels carry different Doppler information across M-dwarf spectral type.
Internal precision is not the same quantity as the RMS of a target time series.
Nightly zero-point correction borrows information from a reference ensemble and requires self-bias safeguards.
Chromatic indices can diagnose activity but do not supply a universal activity correction.
Scaled signal-to-noise precision values are forecasts, not additional achieved survey measurements.

future_analysis.title: CARMENES nightly-zero-point uncertainty replay
future_analysis.status: future analysis question, not completed research and dependent on DR1 metadata
future_analysis.question: How do direct, interpolated and leave-one-target-out nightly zero points change planet-signal recovery in the visible and near-infrared channels?
future_analysis.basis: DR1 publishes velocities and nightly zero points, while later studies identify unresolved few-m/s jumps and wavelength-dependent stellar signals.
steps: Reproduce DR1 nightly zero points with the target-under-test excluded.
Separate direct nightly estimates from adjacent-night replacements.
Propagate zero-point uncertainty into period searches instead of subtracting one fixed value.
Compare VIS, NIR and chromatic-index recovery under identical injection grids.
success_tests: Published DR1 counts and summary statistics reproduce.
No target contributes to its own zero-point correction.
Missing-night interpolation is visible in every output.
Injected amplitudes and false positives are reported by channel.

title: HPF: cryogenic stability, calibration transfer, and wavelength-dependent drift
reading_boundary: Seven selected design, subsystem, commissioning, calibration and illumination sources. It is not a complete HPF planet bibliography.
current_status: The checked HPF project page documents release to full HET science operations in 2019, but a dated 2026 availability source remains open.
short_summary: HPF established stable cryogenic near-infrared spectroscopy with a laser-frequency-comb reference. Its subsystem papers show why one scalar drift is insufficient: thermal control, fibre tracking, detector response, far-field illumination and chromatic etalon evolution contribute differently.
latest_problem: A six-month etalon study measured an average drift near 0.02 m/s/day with local wavelength-dependent departures up to plus or minus 0.05 m/s/day. The nightly calibration scale can therefore be strong while longer transfer requires spectrally resolved monitoring.
lessons: Sub-millikelvin enclosure stability is a subsystem measurement, not stellar precision.
The laser comb can support calibration far below the RMS of a stellar sequence.
Etalon drift is chromatic and cannot always be removed by one nightly scalar.
Large HET pupil changes provide a demanding illumination-transfer test.
A planet non-detection can expose long-period stellar activity that optical data alone misidentified.

future_analysis.basis: Published comb, etalon and far-field studies quantify different calibration-transfer terms over different timescales.
steps: Reproduce the six-month mode-by-mode etalon drift map.
Compare scalar, order-wise and smooth chromatic corrections on held-out date blocks.
Stratify tests by HET pupil geometry and signal-to-noise.

success_tests: Nightly and ten-day calibration scales reproduce within documented definitions.
Held-out improvement exceeds a scalar-drift baseline.
Injected shifts are not absorbed by the chromatic model.
Stellar RMS is never labelled as calibration-only precision.

title: SPIRou: near-infrared velocity, telluric modelling, and magnetic diagnostics
reading_boundary: Five selected target, instrument, telluric, activity and current-operations sources. It is not a complete SPIRou Legacy Survey bibliography.
current_status: CFHT's observer cookbook says SPIRou has been offered since semester 2019A and supplies current observing guidance.
short_summary: SPIRou records YJHK spectra and polarimetry together, providing velocity and magnetic diagnostics from one instrument. Published tests separate excellent internal channel stability from larger stellar scatter shaped by photons, tellurics, persistence and activity.
latest_problem: The instrument paper reports 0.07 m/s in a 32-hour dual-channel calibration test but about 2 m/s for mid-M stellar sequences over weeks. It also identifies detector persistence and faint-target crosstalk or telluric limits.
lessons: Dual-channel calibration stability and stellar time-series RMS answer different questions.
Telluric absorption is dense and variable across the near infrared.
Detector persistence depends on earlier exposures and is most consequential for faint targets.
Polarimetry supplies magnetic information that can constrain, but not automatically remove, activity.
Different line masks probe different magnetic sensitivity and atmospheric contamination.

title: NIRPS: adaptive-optics injection, early sub-m/s results, and sky correction
reading_boundary: Six selected front-end, commissioning, instrument, archive, status and recent methods sources. The 2026 sky-correction item is explicitly a preprint.
current_status: ESO lists NIRPS as offered at the 3.6 m telescope and has released pipeline-reduced spectra from operations beginning in April 2023.
short_summary: NIRPS extends HARPS observations into the near infrared using adaptive-optics-assisted fibre injection and separate efficiency modes. Early work reports selected sub-m/s results, while later sources make mode, sky emission and pipeline version part of the interpretation.
latest_problem: A September 2026 preprint tests night-sky emission corrections separately for high-accuracy and high-efficiency modes. It is recent and should be evaluated as a method proposal rather than settled cross-instrument performance.
lessons: Adaptive optics changes coupling and modal behaviour rather than simply increasing throughput.
An early better-than-1 m/s result belongs to its targets, cadence and commissioning reduction.
High-accuracy and high-efficiency modes should not share one performance label.
Simultaneous HARPS observations enable chromatic tests but require aligned timestamps and models.
Sky-emission correction can remove bias while adding template and subtraction uncertainty.

title: PFS: iodine-cell measurements, configuration eras, and long-baseline use
reading_boundary: Six selected construction, commissioning, science-use, archive and current-roster sources. It is not a complete PFS planet-search bibliography.
current_status: Current Carnegie and Las Campanas pages list PFS as a user instrument on Magellan; Carnegie notes that access is through collaboration with the instrument group.
short_summary: PFS uses the iodine-cell method on the Magellan Clay telescope and has supported decade-scale programmes. Its early below-1 m/s commissioning result belongs to an early configuration, while later science combines different eras, targets and sometimes instruments.
latest_problem: The current institutional page states better-than-1 m/s precision but does not specify the sample, baseline, reduction version or hardware era. The claim therefore remains anchored to the documented commissioning sequence rather than generalized.
lessons: An iodine-cell velocity is relative and depends on the stellar template and line-spread-function model.
The first five-month standard-star RMS cannot represent every later hardware configuration.
Long planet-search baselines gain sensitivity while accumulating instrument and pipeline eras.
Multi-instrument planet fits do not isolate PFS stability by themselves.
A current roster establishes availability, not a complete modern performance characterization.

current_status: The 2026B French call scheduled SOPHIE-RED installation and conditional return to nominal operation; a dated completion report was not identified.

Stable-star repeatability and internal uncertainty are different statistics.
Ensemble zero points need leave-one-star-out validation.
A comb test below 400 nm is a calibration experiment, not stellar precision.
SOPHIE-RED requires its own post-intervention characterization.

Inject long-period and activity-correlated signals.
success_tests: No target contributes to its own correction.
Performance is reported separately by era.
Signal attenuation is bounded by injection tests.
Post-upgrade claims wait for dated data.

title: APF and Levy: iodine modelling, automated cadence, and a dated-status gap
reading_boundary: Four selected instrument, operations and official-page sources; not a complete APF planet bibliography.
current_status: The official Lick page describes APF and Levy, but the checked page does not provide a dated current operational statement.
short_summary: APF couples an automated 2.4 m telescope to the iodine-calibrated Levy spectrograph. Early sub-m/s standards and the later 1.35 m/s median internal uncertainty answer different questions.
latest_problem: The public instrument page establishes the facility but leaves the current status date unresolved.
lessons: Iodine forward modelling ties velocities to templates and line-spread models.
Two first-light standards do not describe a survey distribution.
Median internal uncertainty is not stable-star RMS.
Dynamic scheduling changes cadence and alias structure.
A current instrument page needs a dated availability source.

future_analysis.title: APF cadence and template sensitivity study
future_analysis.status: future analysis question, not completed research
future_analysis.question: How do dynamic cadence and iodine-template choices affect recovery of long-period signals in public APF time series?
future_analysis.basis: The operations literature exposes cadence logic and measurement context, but current configuration metadata must be resolved.
steps: Record schedule, template and reduction eras.
Select standards independently of correction fitting.
Compare actual and cadence-scrambled windows.
Inject signals across period and activity timescales.
success_tests: Templates are never trained on held-out tests.
Cadence effects are separated from noise effects.
Results remain target-specific.
The current-status gap stays visible.

title: iSHELL: gas-cell forward modelling, fringing, and limited RV cadence
reading_boundary: Four selected instrument, RV, archive and current-facility sources; not a complete iSHELL science bibliography.
current_status: IRTF lists iSHELL for 2026B and documents current fringing, flat-field and RV scheduling limits.
short_summary: iSHELL is a general infrared spectrograph with a demonstrated gas-cell RV mode. Published 3 to 5 m/s bright-star results and the facility's broader 10 m/s statement retain their target and baseline contexts.
latest_problem: IRTF states that year-scale RVs are systematics-limited and that only about 25 RV epochs per semester can normally be scheduled.
lessons: General spectral coverage is not an RV precision claim.
Gas-cell results depend on forward-model and template choices.
Fringing makes flat-field cadence part of the measurement.
Bright-star results cannot be assigned to K less than 10 targets generally.
Sparse semester cadence limits long-period validation.

future_analysis.title: iSHELL fringing and cadence sensitivity table
future_analysis.status: future analysis question, not completed research
future_analysis.question: Which flat-field and spectral-order choices dominate gas-cell RV changes under the cadence available in the archive?
future_analysis.basis: The facility documents fringing and year-scale systematics while public data can support bounded replay tests.
steps: Select raw data by programme and date.
Track flats and gas-cell configuration per night.
Hold out orders and observing runs.
Inject signals into raw or forward-model spectra.
success_tests: Fringing choices are reported explicitly.
No 3 to 5 m/s value is generalized beyond its sample.
Cadence aliases are shown.
Public selection is reproducible.

title: IRD: simultaneous comb profiles, telluric forward modelling, and pipeline versions
reading_boundary: Four selected instrument, RV-method, science-use and software sources; not a complete IRD survey bibliography.
current_status: Subaru maintains an official IRD instrument page, but a dated 2026 availability statement remains unresolved in the census.
short_summary: IRD measures near-infrared spectra with simultaneous comb information and segment-wise forward modelling. Below-2 m/s simulations apply to stated stellar and signal-to-noise conditions rather than every observation.
latest_problem: The new PyIRD software record creates a reduction-version boundary whose RV effect has not yet been established on held-out time series.
lessons: Near-infrared tellurics cannot simply be ignored across most of the band.
Instantaneous line-spread profiles are segment-specific.
Simulation precision is not long-term stellar RMS.
Young-star transit RV errors do not characterize stable targets.
Pipeline versions need data-level comparison.

future_analysis.title: IRD telluric and reduction-version replay
future_analysis.status: future analysis question, not completed research
future_analysis.question: How sensitive are recovered RVs to telluric treatment and PyIRD reduction choices across held-out nights?
future_analysis.basis: The published model and new open pipeline expose separable stages for controlled tests.
steps: Create matched legacy and PyIRD reductions.
Bin diagnostics by water vapour and airmass.
Hold out nights and wavelength segments.
Inject shifts before telluric fitting.
success_tests: Simulation and on-sky results remain distinct.
Telluric masks report lost Doppler information.
Version differences are target-specific.
Dated operational status remains unresolved until sourced.

title: PARVI: commissioning measurements and conflicting facility status
reading_boundary: Four selected project, pipeline, commissioning-science and schedule sources; routine facility availability is not established.
current_status: A March 2026 Palomar schedule confirms PARVI hardware use, while current public facility and project pages do not establish routine user availability.
short_summary: PARVI demonstrated single-mode near-infrared commissioning and hot-Jupiter recovery, but its 4 to 10 m/s intra-night scatter did not meet the roughly 1 m/s design aim in that test.
latest_problem: Current evidence supports research-instrument activity, not a settled operational or retired label.
lessons: A design aim must not replace commissioning scatter.
Single-mode injection does not remove detector and calibration errors.
A planet recovery is not an instrument-only stability test.
Scheduled engineering use does not establish facility access.
Conflicting status evidence should remain explicit.

future_analysis.title: PARVI commissioning re-analysis boundary
future_analysis.status: future analysis question, not completed research and dependent on public products
future_analysis.question: Can commissioning data separate injection, calibration and detector terms well enough to reproduce the reported scatter?
future_analysis.basis: Published pipeline methods provide testable diagnostics, but the public data and current access boundary need confirmation.
steps: Inventory released raw and reduced products.
Reproduce per-night scatter before combining nights.
Separate calibrator and stellar light paths.
Inject shifts through extraction and wavelength fitting.
success_tests: The 1 m/s design aim is never plotted as achieved.
Planet-fit residuals remain separate.
Missing products are listed.
Status is not guessed from one page.

title: PARAS-2: on-sky dispersion, fibre scrambling, and thermal-control development
reading_boundary: Four selected instrument, stellar, subsystem and institutional sources; not a complete PARAS-2 science bibliography.
current_status: PRL documents continuing PARAS-2 observations and current coupling, scrambling and detector-cooling development.
short_summary: PARAS-2 has reported a 2.65 m/s daily standard-star dispersion while off-sky inter-fibre drift was much smaller. Current subsystem work shows why these numbers cannot be treated as one precision value.
latest_problem: The double scrambler, Cassegrain module and liquid-nitrogen control remain active engineering boundaries requiring on-sky validation.
lessons: Off-sky inter-fibre drift is not stellar RV precision.
Daily dispersion combines instrument, atmosphere and star.
Coupling and scrambling determine illumination stability.
Thermal targets require measured exposure-level temperatures.
Subsystem changes create dated instrument eras.

future_analysis.title: PARAS-2 light-path error separation
future_analysis.status: future analysis question, not completed research
future_analysis.question: Which part of the gap between off-sky drift and stellar dispersion is explained by illumination, environment and reduction choices?
future_analysis.basis: The published numbers describe different light paths and current subsystem changes provide testable era boundaries.
steps: Align calibration and stellar exposures by time.
Join environmental and guiding diagnostics.
Hold out nights before fitting corrections.
Inject wavelength and illumination perturbations.
success_tests: Light paths are never pooled silently.
Every result carries an era.
Corrections improve held-out nights.
Astrophysical signal recovery is preserved.

title: HARPS3: design requirements and incomplete commissioning
reading_boundary: Four selected design, project and official-status sources; no achieved stellar precision is claimed.
current_status: ING offers 2026B open time on a shared-risk basis and states that commissioning is incomplete.
short_summary: HARPS3 is designed for nightly long-baseline observations with a 0.10 m/s instrumental goal. Current evidence describes integration and shared-risk commissioning, not routine operations or achieved precision.
latest_problem: Availability and performance are explicitly not promised while commissioning remains incomplete.
lessons: A 0.10 m/s value is a design goal.
Ten-year cadence simulations are not observations.
Robotic operations require independent quality controls.
Shared-risk time is not completed commissioning.
The first stable-star sequence must define the achieved baseline.

future_analysis.title: HARPS3 commissioning acceptance table
future_analysis.status: future analysis question, not completed research and blocked on public commissioning data
future_analysis.question: Which tests would distinguish design compliance from achieved nightly and seasonal performance?
future_analysis.basis: The design and current status define required tests, but suitable public measurements are not yet available.
steps: Record hardware and software configuration per commissioning night.
Separate calibration tracking from stellar RMS.
Use standards selected before outcome inspection.
Publish failures and weather exclusions.
success_tests: No requirement is labelled achieved.
Shared-risk caveats remain visible.
All exclusions are machine-readable.
Seasonal performance waits for sufficient baseline.

title: ANDES: science requirements and preliminary-design evidence
reading_boundary: Four selected overview, design, calibration and status sources; ANDES has no achieved on-sky performance.
current_status: The consortium entered system preliminary design review in June 2026, with the review meeting planned for October.
short_summary: ANDES is a planned modular ELT high-resolution spectrograph spanning visible and near-infrared wavelengths. Its precision and coverage values remain requirements at the preliminary-design stage.
latest_problem: Calibration architecture is mature enough for review but has not been built or validated as a complete system.
lessons: Planned coverage is not delivered coverage.
A 0.10 m/s goal is not achieved precision.
Subsystem reviews do not equal system acceptance.
Multiple arms require cross-arm calibration tests.
ELT science cases must not be presented as detections.

Map requirements to calibration and spectrograph subsystems.
Define laboratory and on-sky acceptance measurements.
Track review changes without predicting outcomes.

title: G-CLEF: precision-RV requirements and subsystem construction milestones
reading_boundary: Four selected design and current-project sources; no achieved on-sky performance is claimed.
current_status: G-CLEF remains under development; an August 2026 notice records a blue-camera funding milestone, not completed integration.
short_summary: G-CLEF is a planned visible echelle for GMT with several resolution modes and precision-RV capability. The 0.50 m/s requirement and 0.10 m/s goal are design quantities.
latest_problem: Public milestones refer to individual subsystems and funding, so the full instrument schedule and achieved performance remain open.
lessons: Requirement and goal must be separate fields.
Multiple observing modes have different stability paths.
Exposure-meter design contributes to timing validation.
A funded camera is not a commissioned spectrograph.
On-sky performance depends on the future telescope interface.
